items.title: Why Is Space Black If There Are Billions of Stars? (Olbers' Paradox)
items.description:
Our galaxy alone has hundreds of billions of stars, and there are hundreds of billions of galaxies. So every direction you look should end on a star, and the night sky should blaze like the surface of the Sun. It doesn't. We treat this 400-year-old puzzle, Olbers' paradox, as a case file: four suspects, two cleared, two guilty, and a twist. The sky isn't actually black. The wall of light is still out there, stretched into microwaves.

Chapters
0:00 The sky should be blinding
0:36 The forest problem
1:00 A 400-year-old cold case
1:20 How bright would it be?
1:43 Why the daytime sky is blue
2:08 Suspect 1: far stars are too faint
2:47 Suspect 2: dust
3:22 Suspect 3: the universe has a birthday
4:13 The forest is deeper than we can see
4:32 Stars burn out (and a poet saw it first)
5:21 Suspect 4: space is stretching
6:19 The twist: the sky isn't black
7:20 The darkness is growing
7:50 The verdict
8:10 Next episode

Sources
- NASA Science, Milky Way: 100 to 400 billion stars; NASA / Hubble: hundreds of billions of galaxies in the observable universe
- Olbers' paradox: Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers (1823); Johannes Kepler (1610); Edgar Allan Poe, "Eureka" (1848); Lord Kelvin (1901); Edward Harrison, "Darkness at Night: A Riddle of the Universe" (Harvard University Press, 1987)
- Dust argument fails: absorbed starlight would heat dust until it re-radiates (thermodynamics; see Harrison 1987)
- NASA Science, Andromeda: light takes about 2.5 million years to reach us
- ESA / Planck collaboration: age of the universe about 13.8 billion years; observable universe radius about 46.5 billion light-years
- NASA Science, the Sun: total lifetime about 10 billion years; surface (photosphere) about 5,500 °C
- Edwin Hubble (1929): galaxies recede faster the farther away they are; NASA James Webb Space Telescope observes in infrared to see redshifted distant galaxies
- NASA WMAP / COBE: cosmic microwave background, released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang at about 3,000 K, today 2.725 K; discovered by Penzias and Wilson (1965); roughly 1% of the static on an untuned analog TV
- NASA Apollo: the lunar sky is black at noon because the Moon has no atmosphere; Earth's daytime sky is blue from Rayleigh scattering of sunlight
- NASA / ESA / CSA JWST, JADES-GS-z14-0 (Carniani et al. 2024): redshift about 14.3, light emitted about 290 million years after the Big Bang
- Krauss & Scherrer (2007), General Relativity and Gravitation, "The return of a static universe and the end of cosmology"
- Own calculations (Python): the Sun covers 6.8 × 10^-5 steradians → about 92,500 Suns to tile the half-sky above you; line-of-sight mean free path 1/(nσ) with 10^22 to 10^24 stars in the observable universe → roughly 10^22 to 10^24 light-years; CMB stretch 3,000 K / 2.725 K ≈ 1,100; light stretch 1 + z ≈ 15.3 for z = 14.3

—
Cosmic Scale: the universe, measured in a way you can feel.

Visuals and animations are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.

items.title: Top 5 Brightest Stars in the Night Sky (#2 Is 10,000 Suns) #shorts
items.description:
The five brightest stars at night, and how powerful each one really is. Brightest-looking is not most powerful. Full video on the channel: "Why Is Space Black If There Are Billions of Stars? (Olbers' Paradox)".

Sources
- Hipparcos catalogue (ESA) / NASA: apparent magnitudes Sirius −1.46, Canopus −0.74, Alpha Centauri A+B −0.27, Arcturus −0.05, Vega +0.03
- NASA Science / NASA Imagine the Universe: distances Sirius 8.6 ly, Alpha Centauri 4.37 ly, Vega 25 ly, Arcturus about 37 ly, Canopus about 310 ly
- Luminosities (approximate, stellar catalogues): Sirius A about 25 Suns, Canopus about 10,000 Suns, Arcturus about 170 Suns, Vega about 40 Suns, Alpha Centauri A+B about 2 Suns
- Own calculation: Canopus is about 310 / 8.6 ≈ 36 times farther away than Sirius

Visuals and animations are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
#shorts #space #stars #astronomy

items.title: Earth Fits Inside a Storm on Jupiter. Barely. #shorts
items.description:
Jupiter's Great Red Spot, drawn to scale: about 16,000 km wide, 1.3 Earths. In the 1800s it held about 3. Full video on the channel: "Why Is Space Black If There Are Billions of Stars? (Olbers' Paradox)".

Sources
- NASA / JPL (Juno, 2017): the Great Red Spot measured about 16,000 km (10,159 miles) wide, about 1.3 times Earth's width
- NASA / Hubble (2014): historic observations from the late 1800s gauged the storm as large as about 41,000 km (25,500 miles) on its long axis; observed continuously since at least the 1870s (Simon et al. 2018, Astronomical Journal)
- NASA Planetary Fact Sheets: Jupiter diameter 142,984 km, Earth 12,742 km (Jupiter ≈ 11 Earths wide)
- Own calculation: 16,000 / 12,742 ≈ 1.3 Earths; 41,000 / 12,742 ≈ 3.2 Earths

Visuals and animations are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
#shorts #space #jupiter #planets

items.title: The Night Sky Isn't Actually Black. You Just Can't See It #shorts
items.description:
About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the whole sky was a wall of light. It's still there, stretched about 1,100 times into microwaves. Full video on the channel: "Why Is Space Black If There Are Billions of Stars? (Olbers' Paradox)".

Sources
- NASA WMAP / COBE: cosmic microwave background, released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang at about 3,000 K, today 2.725 K; discovered in 1965 (Penzias and Wilson)
- Own calculation: 3,000 K / 2.725 K ≈ 1,100× stretch

Visuals and animations are original. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
#shorts #space #universe #bigbang
